cues.text: Welcome to Education Session 2: orders and market types.
cues.say: Welcome to Education Session 2: orders and market types.

cues.text: Today: stop loss, take profit, and pending orders. The tools that let you plan and control every trade.
cues.say: Today: stop loss, take profit, and pending orders. The tools that let you plan and control every trade.

cues.text: First, the simplest order: a market order.
cues.say: First, the simplest order: a market order.

cues.text: It opens a trade immediately, at the best available price.
cues.say: It opens a trade immediately, at the best available price.

cues.text: When you buy, you pay the ask price. When you sell, you receive the bid price. The gap between them is the spread.
cues.say: When you buy, you pay the ask price. When you sell, you receive the bid price. The gap between them is the spread.

cues.text: A stop loss is an order that closes your trade automatically, if the price moves against you to a level you choose.
cues.say: A stop loss is an order that closes your trade automatically, if the price moves against you to a level you choose.

cues.text: Its purpose is to limit the loss on a trade, decided in advance, not in the heat of the moment.
cues.say: Its purpose is to limit the loss on a trade, decided in advance, not in the heat of the moment.

cues.text: Example: you buy EUR/USD at 1.1000, with a stop loss at 1.0950, fifty pips away.
cues.say: Example: you buy euro dollar at one point one zero zero zero, with a stop loss at one point zero nine five zero, fifty pips away.

cues.text: On 1 lot, that's a planned maximum loss of about $500.
cues.say: On one lot, that's a planned maximum loss of about five hundred dollars.

cues.text: In fast markets, or when prices gap over a weekend, a stop can be filled at a worse price. This is called slippage.
cues.say: In fast markets, or when prices gap over a weekend, a stop can be filled at a worse price. This is called slippage.

cues.text: Where should a stop go?
cues.say: Where should a stop go?

cues.text: Common practice is to place it where your trade idea is proven wrong. For example, just beyond a recent low, or a support or resistance level.
cues.say: Common practice is to place it where your trade idea is proven wrong. For example, just beyond a recent low, or a support or resistance level.

cues.text: Too close, and normal price noise can stop you out. Too far, and the loss becomes too large.
cues.say: Too close, and normal price noise can stop you out. Too far, and the loss becomes too large.

cues.text: Many traders choose the stop first, and then size the trade.
cues.say: Many traders choose the stop first, and then size the trade.

cues.text: For example, risking 1% of a $10,000 account is $100.
cues.say: For example, risking one percent of a ten thousand dollar account is one hundred dollars.

cues.text: With a 50-pip stop, at $10 per pip per lot, that's 0.2 lots.
cues.say: With a fifty pip stop, at ten dollars per pip per lot, that's zero point two lots.

cues.text: A take profit does the opposite. It closes the trade automatically, when the price reaches your target.
cues.say: A take profit does the opposite. It closes the trade automatically, when the price reaches your target.

cues.text: It locks in the gain, even when you aren't watching the screen, so a winning trade isn't given back.
cues.say: It locks in the gain, even when you aren't watching the screen, so a winning trade isn't given back.

cues.text: Example: you buy at 1.1000, with a take profit at 1.1100. That's 100 pips, about $1,000 on 1 lot.
cues.say: Example: you buy at one point one zero zero zero, with a take profit at one point one one zero zero. That's one hundred pips, about one thousand dollars on one lot.

cues.text: Compared with the 50-pip stop, you risk 50 pips to make 100. That's a risk-to-reward ratio of 1 to 2.
cues.say: Compared with the fifty pip stop, you risk fifty pips to make one hundred. That's a risk to reward ratio of one to two.

cues.text: Targets should fit your strategy. A short-term trader may aim for nearby levels; a longer-term trader, for bigger moves. What matters is that the target is realistic for that market.
cues.say: Targets should fit your strategy. A short-term trader may aim for nearby levels; a longer-term trader, for bigger moves. What matters is that the target is realistic for that market.

cues.text: Now, pending orders.
cues.say: Now, pending orders.

cues.text: A market order trades now. A pending order is an instruction to open a trade later, only if the price reaches a level you set.
cues.say: A market order trades now. A pending order is an instruction to open a trade later, only if the price reaches a level you set.

cues.text: There are four main types.
cues.say: There are four main types.

cues.text: A Buy Limit buys below the current price, when you expect a dip first, and then a rise.
cues.say: A Buy Limit buys below the current price, when you expect a dip first, and then a rise.

cues.text: A Sell Limit sells above the current price, when you expect a rise first, and then a fall.
cues.say: A Sell Limit sells above the current price, when you expect a rise first, and then a fall.

cues.text: A Buy Stop buys above the current price, when you expect a breakout to keep going up.
cues.say: A Buy Stop buys above the current price, when you expect a breakout to keep going up.

cues.text: A Sell Stop sells below the current price, when you expect a breakdown to keep going down.
cues.say: A Sell Stop sells below the current price, when you expect a breakdown to keep going down.

cues.text: An easy way to remember: limit orders look for a better price. Stop orders follow momentum.
cues.say: An easy way to remember: limit orders look for a better price. Stop orders follow momentum.

cues.text: You can attach a stop loss and a take profit to a pending order, so the whole plan is set before the trade even opens.
cues.say: You can attach a stop loss and a take profit to a pending order, so the whole plan is set before the trade even opens.

cues.text: Planning entries in advance has real advantages.
cues.say: Planning entries in advance has real advantages.

cues.text: You don't need to watch the screen. You avoid emotional, last-minute decisions. And every trade starts with a defined risk.
cues.say: You don't need to watch the screen. You avoid emotional, last-minute decisions. And every trade starts with a defined risk.

cues.text: Keep in mind: a pending order may never be triggered, and in fast markets it can be filled at a different price than requested.
cues.say: Keep in mind: a pending order may never be triggered, and in fast markets it can be filled at a different price than requested.

cues.text: Let's recap.
cues.say: Let's recap.

cues.text: A market order trades immediately, at the current price.
cues.say: A market order trades immediately, at the current price.

cues.text: A stop loss limits your loss. A take profit locks in your gain.
cues.say: A stop loss limits your loss. A take profit locks in your gain.

cues.text: Pending orders open trades at the levels you choose: limit orders for a better price, stop orders for momentum.
cues.say: Pending orders open trades at the levels you choose: limit orders for a better price, stop orders for momentum.

cues.say: In session three, we'll look at two advanced strategies: hedging, and averaging.
